m4-t1.question: Why does modern neural TTS sound far more natural than older systems?
options: It plays back recordings of professional actors
It predicts pitch, timing and emphasis from meaning, like other generative models, instead of stitching fragments
It only speaks slowly
It uses louder volume
m4-t1.explanation: Neural TTS learns to predict human-like delivery in context rather than concatenating recorded pieces.

m4-t1.question: Which of these is your main control over pauses and phrasing in TTS?
options: Font size
Punctuation and paragraph breaks in a script written for the ear
File format
The length of the file name
m4-t1.explanation: Commas, full stops and paragraph breaks shape delivery; write for the ear.

m4-t1.question: How should you handle a local place name the voice mispronounces?
options: Accept it
Test, then fix with a phonetic spelling or the tool's pronunciation field
Switch languages
Remove the name
m4-t1.explanation: A pronunciation pass on every proper noun is part of the workflow.

m4-t1.question: What is the recommended pace for a spoken explainer?
options: 60–80 words per minute
140–170 words per minute
250–300 words per minute
As fast as possible
m4-t1.explanation: 140–170 wpm is natural for explainers; slower for instructions.

m4-t1.question: How should you choose a voice for a community announcement?
options: Pick the first default voice
Audition three voices and play the best two to members of the intended audience
Always choose a male voice
Choose the fastest voice
m4-t1.explanation: A voice is a brand choice; the audience's preference matters more than yours.

m4-t1.question: A text-to-speech tool makes a lecture accessible as audio. What should the editor check before sharing?
options: Only whether the audio is loud
Whether the generated voice sounds famous
Nothing because the text is unchanged
Pronunciation, pacing, names, language quality and whether the source text is accurate
m4-t1.explanation: Audio conversion can introduce pronunciation and accessibility issues.

m4-t1.question: A voice sounds natural but does not match the intended audience or purpose. What should guide voice selection?
options: Audience, context, language, tone and consent or licence
The most dramatic voice available
The model’s default choice
The longest sample
m4-t1.explanation: A voice should fit the use and rights constraints.

m4-t1.question: A college wants one announcement in Kannada, Hindi and English. Which workflow is strongest?
options: Translate automatically and publish all versions without review
Prepare reviewed translations, generate short voice samples and ask fluent listeners to check each version
Use English audio for all audiences
Let the model decide the official wording
m4-t1.explanation: Language and pronunciation quality need human review.

m4-t1.question: A generated voice mispronounces a student’s name. What should the producer try?
options: Remove the student’s name from every official notice
Increase the background music
Use an approved phonetic spelling or pronunciation guide and test a short sample
Assume the listener will understand
m4-t1.explanation: Phonetic guidance and sample review can improve pronunciation.

m4-t1.question: A student proposes a podcast for commuters. What audience need is most relevant?
options: A complex chart that cannot be heard
A silent opening
A transcript without audio
Hands-free access, clear pacing and an episode length suitable for the listening context
m4-t1.explanation: Audio format should suit how and where the audience listens.

m4-t1.question: An AI voice uses a confident tone to read uncertain research findings. What should the producer change?
options: Preserve the uncertainty in the script and avoid vocal framing that implies certainty
Remove caveats to improve energy
Increase speaking speed
Add a dramatic soundtrack
m4-t1.explanation: Audio delivery should not exaggerate the evidence.

m4-t1.question: A generated narration includes a product name that is pronounced incorrectly. What is best?
options: Spell the name incorrectly in the published transcript
Check the tool’s pronunciation controls, use a phonetic guide and review the final take
Keep it because the listener can infer it
Add an unrelated jingle
m4-t1.explanation: Named entities should be tested and corrected before publication.

m4-t1.question: An instructor wants audio notes from a lecture. What must be reviewed?
options: Only the audio file size
Whether the voice is synthetic
Transcript completeness, speaker attribution and correctness against the original recording
The colour of the waveform
m4-t1.explanation: Audio summarisation can omit or misattribute important content.

m4-t1.question: A voice tool lets users choose a “celebrity-like” voice. What is the ethical concern?
options: It uses too few tokens
It cannot generate audio
It always lowers accessibility
It could imply endorsement or imitate a real person without consent
m4-t1.explanation: Voice resemblance raises consent and deception risks.

m4-t1.question: Which use of generated speech is a plausible accessibility aid?
options: Offering a reviewed audio version of text with a readable transcript and playback controls
Replacing all written notices
Making audio without a transcript or controls
Using a cloned instructor voice without approval
m4-t1.explanation: Accessible audio should complement text and be checked for quality.

m4-t2.question: What is transcript-based editing?
options: Editing the show notes
Deleting words in the transcript so the audio is cut automatically
Translating the audio
Writing a transcript after editing
m4-t2.explanation: The editor transcribes; you edit text; the audio follows. Always listen back afterwards.

m4-t2.question: What is the risk of maximum-strength noise removal?
options: It deletes the file
The voice becomes watery and robotic
It makes the file larger
It removes the music licence
m4-t2.explanation: Use the lightest setting that works; over-processing smears the voice.

m4-t2.question: How loud should a background music bed be relative to the voice?
options: Equal volume
Louder than the voice
About 15–20 dB below the voice
Silent
m4-t2.explanation: Ducking the bed 15–20 dB under speech keeps the voice intelligible.

m4-t2.question: Which is a legitimate use of voice cloning under the course rules?
options: Cloning a professor's voice for a parody
Cloning your own voice to fix a mispronounced word or produce a Kannada version of your explainer
Cloning a celebrity for a testimonial
Cloning a classmate secretly for a surprise
m4-t2.explanation: Your own voice, or a consenting classmate's with documented consent, labelled as synthetic.

m4-t2.question: What does the lesson recommend to protect your family from cloned-voice scam calls?
options: Never answer the phone
Agree a private safe word and verify by calling back
Post your voice online
Use louder ringtones
m4-t2.explanation: A safe word plus call-back verification defeats urgency-based impersonation.

m4-t2.question: A student wants to clone a relative’s voice after receiving no response to a consent request. What should happen?
options: Do not clone it; use a licensed generic voice or wait for explicit permission
Clone a short sample only
Use a recording from social media
Disclose only after publication
m4-t2.explanation: Silence is not consent for voice cloning.

m4-t2.question: A music generator offers an “in the style of” prompt for a living musician. What is safer?
options: Use the musician’s name to improve similarity
Describe tempo, instrumentation and mood without directing imitation of that musician
Upload unreleased tracks
Remove the artist name after export
m4-t2.explanation: Describe musical attributes rather than copying a living artist’s style.

m4-t2.question: Noise reduction removes background hum but makes speech metallic. What adjustment is appropriate?
options: Apply even stronger noise reduction
Add distortion to the voice
Reduce processing and compare with the untouched recording
Delete the source file
m4-t2.explanation: Preserve the source and choose the least destructive cleanup.

m4-t2.question: A generated music track will appear in a client advertisement. What should the editor verify?
options: Only the beat speed
Whether it sounds original
Whether the tool has a free plan
Licence, commercial rights, attribution and any restrictions on the generated output
m4-t2.explanation: Commercial publication depends on applicable tool and music rights.

m4-t2.question: An audio editor automatically removes pauses and breaths. What can go wrong?
options: It may change meaning, pacing or natural delivery, so edits must be listened to
It makes the voice legally identifiable
It turns all words into text
It guarantees a professional mix
m4-t2.explanation: Automated editing can damage intelligibility or tone.

m4-t2.question: A speaker asks to withdraw voice-cloning consent before the episode is released. What should the team do?
options: Publish because generation already happened
Stop use, remove derived material where feasible and follow the documented consent and retention process
Change only the episode title
Ignore it if the speaker is not named
m4-t2.explanation: Consent should include a clear process for withdrawal and data handling.

m4-t2.question: A clip has a loud hum in one channel only. What is a careful first step?
options: Normalise the entire track to maximum
Remove all bass from both channels
Inspect the channel and make a conservative edit while preserving the original
Add music over the entire recording
m4-t2.explanation: Targeted processing is less destructive than blanket edits.

m4-t2.question: A generated background track sounds similar to a known song. What should the publisher do?
options: Assume AI generation removes copyright concerns
Add a credit to the famous artist
Publish it only on social media
Pause publication and review similarity and rights with an appropriate reviewer
m4-t2.explanation: Generated output can still raise rights concerns.

m4-t2.question: A student edits an interview transcript and removes a sentence that changes the speaker’s meaning. What is the correct practice?
options: Compare edits against the source and preserve meaning, marking any necessary cuts
Keep the cleaner version without review
Replace the quote with a model summary
Delete the recording
m4-t2.explanation: Editing should not distort what the speaker said.

m4-t2.question: Which file-handling practice best protects raw voice recordings?
options: Share the file publicly for convenience
Limit access, retain only as needed, store securely and delete under a stated schedule
Keep every take forever
Upload it to several personal accounts
m4-t2.explanation: Voice data should follow minimisation, access and retention controls.

m4-t3.question: What is the common pattern for every text-to-audio conversion?
options: Copy the document into TTS and export
Plain-language rewrite for the ear → voice → light music → export → verify against the source
Record, then write
Translate word for word
m4-t3.explanation: Re-tell for the ear, produce, then verify facts against the original.

m4-t3.question: Why must AI-drafted meeting minutes be reviewed before circulation?
options: They are too long
Assistants can invent action items nobody agreed to
They are always in English
They lack timestamps
m4-t3.explanation: Announce recording, get consent, and review minutes for invented or misattributed items.

m4-t3.question: Which IVR rule is correct?
options: Offer as many options as possible
State the action before the number, at most four options, always an exit to a human
Prompts should be at least 30 seconds
Never offer a language choice
m4-t3.explanation: Brief greeting, ≤4 options, action-before-number, confirm, exit, language choice.

m4-t3.question: How should transcripts of other people be treated?
options: As public content
As personal data: stored securely, deleted when done, not uploaded to unvetted tools
As marketing material
As permanent records
m4-t3.explanation: Recordings and transcripts are personal data; consent, secure storage and deletion apply.

m4-t3.question: What belongs in show notes?
options: Only the title
Summary, timestamps, links, credits including music licence and AI tools, and a transcript link
The raw audio file
A list of hashtags only
m4-t3.explanation: Show notes support search, accessibility, attribution and disclosure.

m4-t3.question: A written blog becomes a podcast episode. What should not be copied mechanically?
options: The verified central message
Visual references and hyperlinks that listeners cannot use; convert them into spoken context or show notes
Every source title
The disclosure statement
m4-t3.explanation: Audio needs spoken explanations and accessible companion materials.

m4-t3.question: A lecture is converted to study audio. What must be checked before students rely on it?
options: Whether the audio has a cover image
Whether every pause is removed
Key definitions, examples and speaker attribution against the lecture recording
Only the total duration
m4-t3.explanation: Summaries can omit nuance and must be checked against their source.

m4-t3.question: An IVR menu uses AI voices. Which requirement matters most to callers?
options: A theatrical voice
Long policy explanations in every menu
No option to correct a selection
Clear, short instructions with a reliable path to a human or repeat option
m4-t3.explanation: Service audio should be understandable and provide an accessible fallback.

m4-t3.question: A 3-minute episode has no transcript. What important audience need is missed?
options: A text alternative for deaf or hard-of-hearing listeners and for search or reference
A way to increase music volume
A more realistic voice
A larger audio bitrate
m4-t3.explanation: Transcripts support accessibility and later use.

m4-t3.question: A podcast show note contains a link generated by AI that leads to an unrelated site. What should the producer do?
options: Keep it because the URL format looks valid
Open and verify every link and source before release
Shorten it without opening
Ask the same model if it works
m4-t3.explanation: Links should be tested against their intended destinations.

m4-t3.question: A voiceover is mixed so loudly that the music masks speech. What should the editor do?
options: Increase the music further
Add more instruments
Adjust levels and listen on common devices to ensure speech remains clear
Remove captions
m4-t3.explanation: Mixing should preserve speech intelligibility across listening contexts.

m4-t3.question: A campus audio explainer includes a claim from a lecture slide. What should the show notes provide?
options: Only the AI voice model name
No references because it is audio
A generated citation without review
A checked source or reference so listeners can follow the claim
m4-t3.explanation: Audio claims also need traceable sources.

m4-t3.question: A listener has limited bandwidth. What can improve access to the episode?
options: Offer a compressed audio option and transcript without making quality unusable
Require only high-resolution video
Remove all text alternatives
Use the largest file available
m4-t3.explanation: Multiple accessible formats support different devices and connections.

m4-t3.question: A student creates a voiceover for a short video in two languages. What should be reviewed in each version?
options: Only the background music
Timing, meaning, pronunciation, captions and any claims added during translation
Whether the two audio files have identical durations
Nothing after translation
m4-t3.explanation: Translation and audio production can introduce errors that need review.

m4-t3.question: A staff member wants to turn sensitive counselling notes into an audio summary. What should they do?
options: Upload the notes to a personal public voice tool
Use a cloned counsellor voice
Use only an approved, privacy-protective workflow and remove unnecessary personal information
Share the output widely
m4-t3.explanation: Sensitive records require strict data controls and minimisation.

questions.question: A team wants to clone a local shop owner’s voice for a promotion. The owner has not agreed. What should the producer do?
options: Use a generic licensed voice or obtain documented informed consent before any cloning
Clone it because the campaign is positive
Clone it and disclose only in the video description
Use a short sample so consent is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Voice cloning requires consent; a positive purpose or short sample does not replace it.

questions.question: A multilingual voice generator pronounces a Kannada place name incorrectly. What is the best next step?
options: Publish the first take
Translate the place name into English
Increase the background music volume
Write a phonetic pronunciation guide, generate a short test, have a fluent speaker review it, then regenerate the full narration
questions.explanation: Test pronunciations with a fluent reviewer before producing the full asset.

questions.question: A podcast script is 600 words and must fit a three-minute episode. What should the editor do?
options: Speed up the voice until it sounds rushed
Leave the script and remove pauses
Estimate spoken duration, cut to the target word range, then time a real sample read
Add a faster music track
questions.explanation: A realistic read-through catches pace and duration issues before final production.

questions.question: A recording has a hum and a quiet speaker. Which order is safest?
options: Apply maximum denoise, then compress heavily
Keep an untouched source copy, reduce noise gently, level speech, then listen for artefacts
Remove all low frequencies and export immediately
Use music to cover every defect
questions.explanation: Preserve the source and use restrained processing with listening checks.

questions.question: A student wants background music for a public podcast. What should they check before release?
options: The tool’s licence and commercial-use terms, attribution requirements and rights for the intended distribution
Only whether the track sounds appropriate
Whether another podcast used the same track
Nothing if AI generated it
questions.explanation: Generated audio still has tool terms and distribution rights that must be checked.

questions.question: An AI audio overview includes a claim not found in the source reading. What should the learner do?
options: Trust it because the notebook cited a source elsewhere
Add more documents without checking
Ask the audio model to sound less confident
Remove or correct the claim and verify every substantive statement against the supplied documents
questions.explanation: Source-grounded audio can still overstate or introduce content; check against the actual documents.

questions.question: A department creates a lecture-to-podcast workflow. Which hand-off is most useful?
options: A raw voice file only
A prompt history without the final asset
A clean audio file plus checked transcript, source list, episode notes and accessibility-ready captions
An AI confidence score
questions.explanation: A publishable audio package includes accessible text and traceable sources.

questions.question: A student records a peer’s voice for a language lesson. What should happen first?
options: Record secretly and remove the file after generation
Explain the use, get explicit consent, limit the sample and retention, and offer a non-cloned alternative
Ask the AI tool to obtain consent
Use the voice only if the peer is not named
questions.explanation: Consent, data minimisation and an alternative should be built into the workflow.

questions.question: Noise removal makes a speaker’s voice sound metallic. What is the appropriate quality-control response?
options: Back off processing, compare with the original and accept some background noise rather than damage speech
Increase the denoising amount
Add reverb to hide the artefact
Export at a higher bitrate only
questions.explanation: Over-processing harms intelligibility; compare against the source and use the least destructive settings.

questions.question: A 60-second campus audio clip will be repurposed into a podcast, reel and accessible web page. What should remain consistent?
options: Only the file name
The exact same crop and intro everywhere
The AI voice regardless of audience
The verified core message and facts, adapted per format with captions, context and appropriate rights checks
questions.explanation: Repurposing adapts the format while preserving verified claims and accessibility.
